name: Stroop effect
statement: Naming the ink colour of a printed colour word is slowed when the word names a different colour, while reading the word is barely slowed by the ink.
meaning: The interference runs one way. A skilled reader cannot look at the word 'red' without reading it, so when the task is to say the ink colour instead, the wrong answer arrives first and has to be held back. Reversing the task removes almost all of the cost: an incongruent ink colour does little to the speed of reading the word. That asymmetry is the finding, and it is usually taken as evidence that reading has become automatic while colour naming has not. The effect is measured as a difference score, the incongruent condition minus a control condition, and that scoring choice matters more than it looks.

origin.note: The paper is "Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions", submitted as a doctoral thesis at George Peabody College and received by the journal on 15 August 1934. Stroop was writing about interference in general and gave his materials no name; the label came from later authors.

evidence: Stroop ran three experiments with printed cards, not single trials, and timed each card with a stop watch. The colours were red, blue, green, brown and purple, arranged so that no word appeared in the colour it named. Experiment 1 asked 70 undergraduates, 14 men and 56 women, to read colour names aloud, once printed in conflicting inks and once in black. Each subject read two sheets of each test, 200 reactions per test, and the times are quoted per 100 words. The conflicting inks cost 2.3 seconds, 5.6% of the black-print time, which Stroop called not reliable at D/PEd = 3.64. MacLeod's table of that experiment gives 43.30 seconds against 41.00. Experiment 2 switched the task to naming the ink colours, with solid colour squares as the control, and used 100 students: 88 undergraduates, 29 men and 59 women, and 12 graduate students, all women. Mean time for 100 responses rose from 63.3 seconds to 110.3, an increase of 47.0 seconds or 74.3%, with medians of 61.9 and 110.4. The standard deviation rose from 10.8 to 18.8, leaving the coefficient of variability unchanged at .171. The gap of 47 seconds was 4.35 standard deviations of the control condition and 2.5 of the interference condition. Stroop added twice the average time per word for each uncorrected error, a correction he called arbitrary, which moved the two means from 108.7 and 63.0. Experiment 3 recruited 32 University of Arizona undergraduates, 17 men and 15 women, for eight days of practice at naming ink colours, 200 reactions a day. Three of them are absent from the results: two were dropped for not keeping to the schedule, and one woman's data were discarded after Ishihara testing showed red-green trouble. The control card changed too, from solid squares to swastikas, so that white would appear beside the colour as it does in print. Colour naming under conflicting words improved by 16.8 seconds, 33.9% of the first day's mean, while the plain colour-naming control improved by only 4.0 seconds or 13.9%. Those third-experiment times are for cards of 50 words rather than the 100 of the first two experiments, so the gain runs from 49.6 seconds to 32.8, on MacLeod's reading of Stroop's tables. Practice also made reading harder. Taking the same figures from MacLeod, reading words in conflicting colours went from 19.4 seconds before the practice series to 34.8 seconds after, and back to 22.0 seconds after one day of reading practice. Those are card times, not interference scores.

replication.headline: Many Labs 3 obtained the effect in every one of its 21 samples, d = 0.88 across 3,337 people, with heterogeneity between sites near zero.
replication.detail: Ebersole and 63 colleagues ran ten effects in 20 university participant pools, N = 2,696, and one online sample, N = 737. The Stroop task was the strongest of them. Its row in their table of results gives an aggregate d = 0.88, 95% CI [0.84, 0.92], t = 49.795, df 3,336, N = 3,337, p < .001, with a median site estimate of 0.89 and a meta-analytic estimate of 0.91, 95% CI [0.84, 0.98]. The same table puts the proportion of samples with a positive effect at p < .05 at 1.00, and the proportions for a reversal and for a null at 0.00. The running text describes the identical comparison as N = 3,279, t(3,336) = 50.22, so the paper's two accounts of the sample disagree. Heterogeneity was near the floor, Q(20) = 15.1883, p = .7655, I-squared = 4.05%. Scoring moves the size: a secondary analysis on the mean difference of log-transformed data gave t(3,347) = 44.17, d = .76, 95% CI [.72, .80]. The error rates moved with the times. Participants made 1.6 percentage points more errors on incongruent trials, t(3,337) = 18.52, d = .32, 95% CI [.29, .36]. The task was a shortened computerised version scored by the D algorithm, and a footnote records fewer colours and trials than most research applications, so a smaller though still large effect was expected. The original effect size they compared against, d = 2.04, is not Stroop's own figure. It is the young-adult aggregate from Verhaeghen and De Meersman's meta-analysis of 20 studies contained in 15 articles. Their abstract puts older adults at d = 2.17, gives no interval for either figure, and concludes that the age sensitivity of Stroop interference is an artefact of general slowing, a single Brinley regression line with a slowing factor of 1.9 fitting the data at R-squared = .83. The interval printed beside 2.04 in Many Labs 3, 95% CI [1.90, 2.18], is that project's own: its table note says intervals for original effect sizes were computed from cell sample sizes. The full text of the meta-analysis was not obtained, so nothing beyond its abstract is quoted here. MacLeod repeated Stroop's first two experiments and reports the data in his 1991 review as MacLeod (1986), unpublished raw data. With 50 subjects he found no interference from incongruent colours in word reading, 41.58 seconds against 41.16, F(1, 49) = 1.86, p = .17, matching Stroop's null. With 40 subjects naming ink colours he found 102.27 seconds against 59.76, F(1, 39) = 363.65, p < .001. Both experiments came out where Stroop left them, half a century later. The largest recent pooling is by Otsuka, Ueda and Saiki, who meta-analysed 737 samples from 399 articles using the colour-word test. That paper is paywalled at Sage, which returned 403 to every request on 17 August 2026, and OpenAlex lists no repository copy, so only the abstract deposited at Crossref was read. It reports larger reaction-time effects in Asia than in North America and Europe and no regional difference on accuracy measures, and no pooled overall estimate is quoted here because none was reachable.

study.cite: Ebersole, C. R., et al. (2016). Many Labs 3: Evaluating participant pool quality across the academic semester via replication. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 67, 68-82.

limits: The group effect is close to unbreakable. The measure of one person is not. Hedge, Powell and Sumner gave seven classic tasks to undergraduates twice, sessions three weeks apart, across three studies that recruited 50, 62 and 42 people. The Stroop task ran in the first two, where 47 and 56 participants survived the compliance criteria. Reliabilities across the seven tasks ranged from 0 to .82. The Stroop reaction-time cost was among the better ones, at ICC = .60, 95% CI [.31, .78], and ICC = .66, 95% CI [.26, .83]. It still sat below its own ingredients. Congruent trials scored .77 and .72, incongruent trials .67 and .70. Subtracting one condition from the other strips out the between-person variance a correlation needs and leaves the noise. The authors write that no behavioural measure in those two studies exceeded .8. In the third study the highest figure was the Navon local error cost at .82, 95% CI [.69, .90], and the lowest was the Navon global reaction-time cost at 0, 95% CI [0, .18]. Their argument is that the two properties are the same property. An effect becomes famous because people differ little in it, and a measure ranks people badly for the same reason. MacLeod had already recorded the pattern in 1991, citing Harbeson and colleagues on a group Stroop test whose individual card times were reasonably reliable and whose derived difference scores were not. His own summary that year was that the colour-word test has reasonable reliability and validity as a psychometric tool, which is the judgement the later work revises. Enkavi and colleagues found the same shape at scale, with a median test-retest ICC of 0.311 for behavioural task measures in 150 people against 0.674 for self-report surveys, at a median gap of 115 days. The consequence is practical. A Stroop difference score is a poor input to any study correlating attention with brain structure, personality or diagnosis, however certain the underlying effect is. The emotional Stroop, in which the words are threatening rather than colour names, is a separate literature with a separate record and is treated below.
misreadings: Most descriptions of the 1935 paper are wrong about it. MacLeod, who read the whole literature for his review, lists the errors. People write as though one experiment contrasted four conditions, when the four cards come from two separate experiments. The word-reading data of Experiment 1 usually go unmentioned. Stroop is credited with a congruent condition of colour words in matching inks, which he never used, and with timing single stimuli, which he never did. His paper contains no theory of automaticity, and it does contain the first report of the reverse effect. The second misreading concerns what the task measures. MacLeod titled a 1992 commentary "The Stroop task: The 'gold standard' of attentional measures". The count sits in his 1991 review, which put the literature in excess of 700 articles and at least 300 of them using Stroop interference as a measure of attention in individual differences, drug effects and the like. The reliability work above is the reason to be careful with that use. A task can produce the same effect in every laboratory on earth and still fail to tell one person from another. Reading the task as a window into what somebody is preoccupied with is the third error, and the emotional Stroop is where it happens. The threat-bias literature that version belongs to is treated in Attentional bias, entry 207, and its figures are not restated here. Phaf and Kan pooled 70 published emotional Stroop studies. The largest effects came from blocked presentation of threat words, which they read as slow interference rather than a fast automatic bias. They found no evidence of interference under suboptimal, less conscious presentation, and significant effects only in fully conscious conditions among high-anxious non-clinical participants and patients. Joyal and five colleagues later pooled 47 studies, 54 datasets and 1,068 healthy controls in patient groups. Interference by diagnosis-related words was reliable in all three, g = .65 in post-traumatic stress disorder, g = .36 in major depression and g = .30 in anxiety disorders. Generally negative words moved depression, g = .58, and anxiety, g = .32, but not post-traumatic stress disorder, g = .33, p = .139. Fisk and Haase ran the masked version online with 45 people and the unmasked version with 50, and found nothing either way, t(49) = .56, p = .58, d = .08 on the unmasked test. Their masked conditions returned Bayes factors of 4.9, 3.5 and 5.2 in favour of the null. By their own power analysis those conditions had 35% to 40% power for the expected 20 millisecond effect, against 80% for the unmasked one, and their discussion gives the first experiment's sample as 44 where the method section gives 45. Eide and colleagues had already shown the reliability problem here. Testing 33 people a week apart, reaction times in each emotion condition retested well and the interference indices did not. Nothing in the colour-word literature licenses using the task to detect a guilty conscience or a hidden concern in an ordinary person.
